name: Toompea Castle
label: Toompea Castle
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3502552: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Toompea Castle' (170 m across).

text.description: Toompea Castle sits on top of Toompea hill in central Tallinn, and today it is home to the Parliament of Estonia, the Riigikogu. It photographs well because several different eras stand side by side. The medieval walls and towers date largely from the 13th century onwards. A large Baroque and Neoclassical wing was added in the eastern part of the complex after Russia took over in 1710, and a separate parliament building from 1922 stands on the site of the old convent building. The tallest tower, Tall Hermann (Pikk Hermann), is 48 metres high and dominates the skyline. The Estonian flag is raised on it every day at sunrise and lowered at sunset, which gives you a good reason to time a visit. The hill is also the subject of a 19th-century legend that the heroine Linda built it boulder by boulder. For photos, think of this as a building to frame in layers: a wide view of the long façade, then closer shots of the stonework and, if it is in view, the tower. Keep your phone level so the walls and tower stay straight, and take a few frames with and without people in them for scale. Right next to it: Alexander Nevsky Cathedral.
text.geographic_location: On Toompea hill in the central part of Tallinn.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from central Tallinn and head up towards Toompea hill, by taxi or hired scooter if you prefer not to walk. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole façade, then switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are too close to fit the wing in. If Tall Hermann is in view from where you stand, use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for it and for details of the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the walls and tower with the vertical lines so they do not lean. Include a little foreground, such as paving or a path, to give a sense of scale, and use the telephoto to isolate a single stretch of wall, or the tower if it is in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus and drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a quick burst or Live Photo if people are crossing your frame, so you can pick the cleanest moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around sunrise or sunset, when the flag is raised or lowered on Tall Hermann. Soft early or late light usually flatters the stonework, but check how the light falls on the day.

text.access_note: The castle houses the working Parliament of Estonia, so the exterior can be photographed from outside, but check the official site before you go for any visiting rules inside.

name: Seaplane Harbour
label: Seaplane Harbour
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lennusadam' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Lennusadam' (way/813621271): edge nearest the subject (984 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Seaplane Harbour'.

text.description: Seaplane Harbour (Lennusadam) is a maritime museum that opened in spring 2012, set in a building first put up as a hangar for seaplanes. It stands in the area of Peter the Great's Naval Fortress. The hall covers 8,000 m2 and was taken out of service in the Soviet era, and its renovation began in 2010. That history is why the place photographs well: big, plain hangar shapes sit right beside the water, and old ships are moored along the harbour edge. The museum's best-known exhibit is the 1936 submarine Lembit, and the icebreaker Suur Tõll is another of its historic vessels. Walk along the water's edge for a few steps before you shoot, because small changes in position change what lines up with the hangar. For a second angle, the Noblessner marina promenade across the cove shows the arched hangars with a grey warship moored in front of them. If you also walk to the museum itself, the open-air pier behind it is an optional extra viewpoint, with moored ships close by for the foreground. Inside the museum the hangar is dim, so plan to take your best pictures outdoors.
text.geographic_location: Seaplane Harbour is on Tallinn's waterfront, north of the city centre, in the old Peter the Great's Naval Fortress area. The museum building was originally a seaplane hangar and sits right on the harbour edge.
text.directions_text: From central Tallinn, head north towards the waterfront and ask for Lennusadam (Seaplane Harbour). Once you have your shot, you can optionally walk to the museum and out onto the open-air pier behind it as an extra viewpoint. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the hangar, the water and the sky together. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the hangar curves and roofline closer from this distance. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you walk to the museum itself and the roofline will not fit.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (harbour side and the open-air pier behind the museum). The museum's hangar hull and seaplanes, with historic ships moored along the harbour edge in the foreground. The museum lies to the south-west of you, so face that way. From this distance the hangar hull and roofline appear as a distant shape across the water. If you walk to the museum, the open-air pier behind it is a separate, closer viewpoint where moored ships can make the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines, keep the horizon level, and place the hangar hull on one of the vertical lines with the water filling the lower third. If you want a different view, the Noblessner marina promenade across the cove shows the arched hangars with a grey warship in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the hangar to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright so the building does not turn into a silhouette. Don't expect good results inside the dim hangar; if you shoot indoors, use night mode and hold still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light in the early morning or late afternoon usually flatters the hangar and the water, but the spot works in most daylight.

text.access_note: The museum itself is ticketed, but you can photograph from the public waterfront; check the official site before you go for current access and ticket details.

name: Kadriorg Palace
label: Kadriorg Palace
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/8073278: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kadriorg Palace' (59 m across).

text.description:
Kadriorg Palace is a pale Baroque building that Peter the Great had built for his wife Catherine. Work began in 1718 and the main building was finished by 1725. Both its Estonian and German names mean "Catherine's valley". It photographs well because it is a single, well-proportioned building with a clear outline, set in a park, so there is little clutter around it.

The palace fell into neglect during the 20th century. After Estonia regained independence, restoration began in 1991 with Swedish government support, and it reopened to the public in 2000. Today it houses the Kadriorg Art Museum, which shows foreign art from the 16th to the 20th century. Estonian art is shown at Kumu, a short way off in the same park.

For your photo, stand back and keep the whole building in the frame, with a strip of the grounds in front of it to give a sense of scale. Turn on gridlines and line up the roofline with a horizontal line so the palace doesn't look tilted. If other visitors walk through the scene, take a few shots a few seconds apart and keep the best one. Tap the palace to set focus and lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky looks too bright.
text.geographic_location: Kadriorg Palace stands in the Kadriorg district of Tallinn, in the park that surrounds it. The Kumu art museum is nearby in the same park.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. From central Tallinn the simplest way is by taxi or hired scooter to Kadriorg; ask for Kadriorg Palace (Kadrioru loss). The phone icon on the map is about 25 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which should take in the whole width of the palace from where you stand. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground, and keep the palace central so the edges don't stretch. Use telephoto (2x or more) for details such as the roofline or windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 25 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone level and switch on gridlines. Put the palace in the middle third and leave some grass or path in the lower part of the frame. For a second shot, step a little to one side so the building sits at an angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the walls don't wash out. If it is crowded, Live Photos can help you pick a frame with fewer people in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. At midday you will be shooting towards the sun, so the front of the palace may look dark against a bright sky.

text.access_note: The palace is a museum, so interior access and opening arrangements may vary; check the official site before you go.

name: Viru Gate
label: Viru Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Musumägi' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Musumägi' (way/8073173): middle (170 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6522415: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description: Viru Gate is a pair of round towers with red conical roofs, ranked 4 on the Tallinn map. The towers have a strong, simple shape. At their base the flower stalls add colour, and the ivy looks best from the park side. Most people shoot it from street level, so frames are often full of passers-by. This spot suggests a different angle. A short staircase leads up from the gate area into Musumägi, a hill park. From there you look at the gate from above and slightly to the side, with the towers rising over the crowds below. Guides describe this as a quieter, elevated alternative, and some call it an underrated photo spot. They disagree about the best side: one favours the park side, where the ivy looks best, and another prefers the flower-shop side. Try both if you have a minute. The flower stalls are seasonal and busy in peak season, so expect people in the lower part of the frame. The towers cannot be entered, so take your photos from outside. Musumägi is a hill park, so expect some uneven steps and watch your footing while you hold your phone up. Take a few frames with different amounts of the towers and the street in them, then pick your favourite later.
text.geographic_location: Viru Gate is on the Tallinn map. The Musumägi park viewpoint is just beside it.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Viru Gate in Tallinn. Once at the gate, take the short staircase up into Musumägi park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show both towers and a little of the street. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the red roofs and cut down the crowds. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you step closer and want the whole height of the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Musumägi (short staircase up from the gate area; elevated viewpoint). The gate from above and at an angle, with the towers seen over the crowds at street level. Up the short staircase from the gate area. You look down on it at an angle, with the towers rising above the people at street level.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the two towers on one vertical line, leaving the street or the flower stalls in the lower third. Try a second shot with the ivy in the foreground. If you want the classic view with the flower stalls framing the base of the towers, look at the street-level viewpoint at Viru värav as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the towers to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the red roofs keep their colour. If the steps are busy, hold the phone steady with both hands and take a few frames.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the park and gate area are quieter, and check the light on the day, as the angle changes through the seasons. The flower stalls are seasonal and busy in peak season.

text.access_note: The park viewpoint and gate area are open outdoor public space, the towers cannot be entered, and you should check the official site before you go for any local changes.

name: Telliskivi Creative City
label: Telliskivi
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Telliskivi Loomelinnak' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/419976748: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Telliskivi Creative City is a district of converted industrial buildings, and its main entrance is a much-photographed spot. At the gate at Telliskivi 60a (Telliskivi Loomelinnak) you look into a courtyard through a brick gateway, with a bold mural on the wall beside it. The red brick and bright paint make a strong, simple frame, and the gateway gives your picture a clear foreground and a sense of walking in.

Because it is so often photographed, it works well as an opening frame for your visit. Start here, then wander in and photograph the courtyards and brickwork at your own pace.

Murals and courtyard art are repainted often, so the one you see may differ from older photos you have found online. Treat the mural as a colourful backdrop rather than the one thing you came for. The gateway, the brick and the courtyard beyond will still give you a good picture.

If you want a second view, Fotografiska Tallinn is recommended for an elevated look over the rust-red roofs of the complex toward the medieval skyline. Telliskivi tänav gives a street-level view of the converted buildings and their brickwork. Access to Fotografiska may depend on the museum or restaurant being open, so check before you go.

Take a few frames from slightly different heights and distances. A step or two to either side changes how much of the mural and gateway you capture.
text.geographic_location: In Tallinn, in the Telliskivi creative district, at the main entrance gate on Telliskivi street (Telliskivi 60a).
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use your map app to find Telliskivi 60a. Type 'Telliskivi Loomelinnak' or the street address into the app. Once there, the phone icon on the map is at the entrance gate itself, so there is no extra walk from the drop-off. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole gateway, mural and courtyard in one frame. The default lens (1x) gives a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. Use 2x or the telephoto to pick out a section of the mural or brickwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see the courtyard entrance with its bold mural and brick gateway, framing the creative district as you walk in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and centre the gateway so the brick gateway frames the courtyard beyond. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines of the walls stay straight. Leave room for the mural on one side. If you want a different view, Fotografiska Tallinn offers an elevated look over the rust-red roofs, and Telliskivi tänav gives a street-level view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the mural to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the colours stay rich and the brick does not wash out. Try a Live Photo if people are walking through the gateway, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the courtyard is lit and you can see the mural colours clearly.

text.access_note: The entrance and courtyard are the stand-here point, but nearby venues such as Fotografiska may have their own opening times and ticket rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Kohtuotsa viewing platform
label: Kohtuotsa viewpoint
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/557300914: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description: Kohtuotsa viewing platform is a lookout in Tallinn, and the reason to come is the view over the city. Platforms like this work well for phone photographers because any edge or foreground feature of the platform can give the picture a clear foreground, middle and far distance. It is easy to fit into a walk, since you only need a few minutes to take a handful of good frames. Then walk up to the edge for the view itself. Hold the phone level, switch on gridlines and line the horizon up with one of the lines, so the scene does not lean. Keep a little of any edge or foreground feature of the platform in the frame if you want the picture to feel like a real place rather than a postcard. If other visitors are in the way, wait a moment: people come and go quickly at viewpoints. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, because the same view gives a very different picture at 0.5x and at 2x or more. Check the screen for fingerprints on the lens before you start.
text.geographic_location: Kohtuotsa viewing platform is in Tallinn.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot; check a local map for the best way to get there. The phone icon on the map is about 15 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Begin with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the platform and the whole view, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out distant details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 15 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. Take a first frame from here, then walk to the platform for the view itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line. Include a little of the platform edge or other foreground element for depth. Try one frame in portrait orientation and one in landscape, since the view suits both.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sky or a point in the view to focus, then use the exposure slider to pull the brightness down a little so the sky keeps its colour. If the scene looks flat, a gentle panorama sweep can capture the full width of the view.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light early or late in the day usually flatters the view, and a clear day gives the longest view. Early in the morning there are likely to be fewer people.

text.access_note: Access and any restrictions are not stated here, so check the official site or local signs before you go.

name: St. Olaf's Church
label: St. Olaf's Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Patkuli vaateplatvorm' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Patkuli vaateplatvorm' (node/60687756): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/26889368: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St Olaf's Church' (81 m across).

text.description:
St. Olaf's is the tallest church building in Estonia, and from the cliff edge of Toompea its spire rises behind the Old Town walls and towers. That is why it photographs so well. You get stone towers in the foreground, a long slim spire behind them, and the church looks small and far away, which suits a postcard-style frame. Local postcards show this same view most often.

The church is a Baptist church today. It was Catholic first, then Lutheran after the Reformation. Its first written mention is from 1267, and the spire now stands at about 124 metres. From 1944 until 1991 the Soviet KGB used the spire as a radio tower and lookout. A local legend says the builder was a stranger named Olev who fell from the tower when the townspeople shouted his name.

For your photo, use the Toompea cliff-edge viewpoint area. The walls and towers fill the lower half of the frame, and the spire stands up out of the middle. Turn on the gridlines and keep the spire on one of the vertical lines so it stays upright. If the area is busy, Kohtuotsa is another viewpoint on Toompea. It shows the spire above the red Old Town roofs, and in some frames the Baltic Sea behind. The tower's observation platform sits at 60 metres, but it looks down on the city rather than at the church, so it won't give you this picture.
text.geographic_location: St. Olaf's stands in Tallinn's Old Town, to the north-east of Toompea hill. The Toompea cliff edge looks down over the Old Town walls towards it, and Patkuli is a viewpoint nearby.
text.directions_text: From there the church lies about 500 m to the north-east, if you want to walk down for a closer look. The spire is easy to spot, so keep it ahead of you as you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start on the default lens (1x) to take in the walls, towers and spire together. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the spire closer and compress the layers. Skip the ultra-wide (0.5x) here, because it makes the spire tiny.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Patkuli vaateplatvorm (Toompea cliff edge above the Old Town walls). The classic postcard view of the city walls and towers in the foreground, with St. Olaf's spire rising behind them. From there you look over the Old Town walls and towers, with St. Olaf's spire rising behind them to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the towers and wall in the lower part of the frame and let the spire rise out of the middle. Switch on the gridlines and keep the spire vertical. If the area is too busy, Kohtuotsa vaateplatvorm, another viewpoint on Toompea, gives a different view, with the spire above the red roofs.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the spire to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stone walls don't go too bright. Hold the phone steady with both hands and rest your elbows on the railing if there is one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually calmer, and the light is softer. Patkuli and Kohtuotsa can be crowded, so go early if you want the viewpoint to yourself.

text.access_note: The Patkuli viewpoint is an open public terrace, but St. Olaf's is a working church and the tower climb is paid and may be closed for renovation, so check the official site before you go.

name: Town Hall Square
label: Town Hall Square
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4061219: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Town Hall' (49 m across).

text.description:
Town Hall Square is the medieval market square at the heart of Tallinn's Old Town, and the Town Hall on its south side is what gives it character. The building is made of grey limestone with a clay-tiled roof. It is the oldest town hall in the Baltic Sea region and Scandinavia, and the last surviving Gothic town hall in Northern Europe. The slim octagonal tower rises 64 metres, with a baroque spire topped by the weather vane Old Thomas (Vana Toomas), which has been a symbol of Tallinn since 1530. The Old Town, including the Town Hall, has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1997.

It photographs well because the square is wide and open, so you can step back and fit the whole tall tower in the frame. The long arcade along the front and the steep roof give you strong lines to work with. The building is also slightly crooked, because it was extended in stages over several centuries, which is part of its charm.

Hold your phone upright to catch the full height of the spire, then try a landscape shot to include the square and the buildings around it. Take a few frames, since people will wander through.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Town (Vanalinn) of Tallinn, on the south side of the medieval Town Hall Square. Kullassepa street, Dunkri street and Vanaturu kael all lead onto the square.
text.directions_text: Head for Tallinn Old Town, then walk to Town Hall Square. Follow the open square eastwards and the tower will guide you. The phone icon on the map is about 60 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole Town Hall and tower. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the full square and the arcade, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the spire and the Old Thomas weather vane.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 60 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. The Town Hall and its tower sit straight ahead.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so the spire does not lean. Keep your phone upright and level, as tilting it back makes the building lean inwards. For a second picture, zoom in on the spire and the weather vane against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Town Hall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail. Avoid 0.5x close to the building, because it stretches the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the square. In the evening, try night mode with your phone held steady against something solid.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the Town Hall itself works as a museum and concert venue, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: The square is open and free to walk around at any time.
Early morning or late afternoon usually has softer light and fewer visitors.
From the west side of the square you look east towards the Town Hall and its tower, with its long front facing the square.
Tilting the phone up toward a tall building makes the vertical lines lean inwards.

name: Kumu Art Museum
label: Kumu
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'KUMU' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kumu' (node/344390065): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/26882906: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Kumu is Tallinn's art museum, set in Kadriorg Park, and its building is as good a photo subject as anything inside it. The front is curved and made of pale limestone and glass. The glass picks up the sky and the trees of the park, so the picture changes with the weather and with where you stand. Visitor guides single out the exterior as a subject in its own right, and say it looks different from each angle. That makes the park-side approach, looking at the curved front, the standard shot and a good place to start.

On a phone, the curve is the main thing to show. Stand back far enough to let the line of the wall sweep across the frame, and include a little sky and some park so the reflections make sense. Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level, because the pale stone shows up any tilt. Once you have the full front, walk closer and take a second photo of a detail, such as the join between stone and glass or a reflection of the trees.

There is also an open-air courtyard framed by the building's curved limestone walls, with bronze and modern sculptures. It makes a good second photo if you go inside. The courtyard needs a museum ticket, and it is open on Mondays only in summer, through 30 September. Flash is not allowed, tripods are discouraged, and some temporary exhibitions ban photography, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Kumu stands in Kadriorg Park, Tallinn.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot. Head for Kadriorg Park and follow the paths to the museum. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole curved front in from fairly close. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view from further back. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a close-up of the stone and glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (park-side approach, facing the curved facade). The curved pale limestone and glass front of the museum, with the sky and the park reflected in it. Walk on along the park-side approach for the close view. From here the photo shows the curved pale limestone and glass front, with the sky and the park reflected in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the base of the building up with a horizontal line so the curve does not look tilted. Leave a band of sky and some park in the frame so the reflections show. If you go into the courtyard, a second photo of its curved limestone walls with the sculptures in front works well as an alternative to the outside shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the glass part of the facade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky reflections keep their detail and the pale stone does not turn white. Do not use flash, as it is not allowed inside.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sky has some cloud or colour, since the glass reflects it. Soft daylight is kinder to the pale stone than harsh midday sun.

text.description:
Fat Margaret is a squat, round defensive tower at the harbour end of Tallinn's Old Town, and it is one of the most solid-looking buildings in the city. It was built between 1511 and 1530 as part of the rebuilt gate defences. The walls are about 25 metres across, 20 metres high and up to 5 metres thick, which is where the name comes from. It was also meant to impress people arriving by sea. Over the centuries it has been a gunpowder and weapons store and a prison, and since the reconstruction of 1978 to 1981 it has housed the Estonian Maritime Museum.

It photographs well because of its simple, heavy shape. A smartphone picture works best when you show the whole drum rising from something soft. The park at the foot of the tower does this well. From there the full round bulk of the tower stands above the lawn and trees, with the old town wall running alongside. One guide suggests the tower looks better from this park side than from the port side, where it was once meant to be seen. For a tighter, more upright picture, walk to Müürivahe. There the tower's face rises straight above the narrow lane, framed by the wall and nearby towers.

Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean inwards, and leave a little space around the top of the tower. Passers-by often wander through the park, so take a few frames and pick the clearest one.
text.geographic_location: In Tallinn's Old Town, at the seaward end of Pikk tänav (Long Street), beside the town wall and close to the Great Coastal Gate. A park lies at the foot of the tower.
text.directions_text: Walk to the harbour end of Pikk tänav in the Old Town; the tower is the big round building there. The spot is reached on foot within the Old Town. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the green space at the foot of the tower to show the whole tower. If the tower is too big for the frame, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), which also suits the narrow Müürivahe lane. Telephoto (2x-5x) is useful for the stonework and the upper wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Margareeta aed (the green space at the foot of the tower). The full round bulk of the tower rising from the lawn and trees at its base, with the old town wall beside it. The tower is to the north-west of you. From here the photo shows the full round bulk of the tower rising from the lawn and trees at its base, with the old town wall beside it. The green space at the foot of the tower gives the best view of the tower itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the phone upright so the walls stay straight. Put the tower on one of the grid's vertical lines and let the lawn and trees fill the foreground. For a more vertical shot, try the alternative at Müürivahe, where the facade rises above the narrow lane between the wall and nearby towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower's stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its colour and the sky is not washed out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the stonework more than harsh midday sun.

text.description: St Nicholas' Church (Niguliste kirik) is one of the medieval landmarks of Tallinn's Old Town. Its tall tower and spire stand out above the rooftops of the Lower Town. The church was built around 1230-1275 by Westphalian merchants and was dedicated to Saint Nicholas, the patron of fishermen and sailors. The tower is now 105 metres high. A Baroque spire replaced the earlier one in the late 17th century, and the tower and spire were damaged by fire in 1982 and then restored. The church was badly damaged by bombing on 9 March 1944 and was restored over many years. Today it is the Niguliste Museum and a concert hall. Its best-known artwork is Bernt Notke's Danse Macabre. The best photo is taken from a distance, because from the church itself the spire is hard to fit into the frame. From the terrace at Kohtuotsa on the Upper Town side you look down on the spire and the Old Town roofs, with the Toompea hill around them. That makes a layered picture with the church as the clear centre. The terrace is a popular viewing spot, so expect to share the railing at busy times. If you want a second angle, the Danish King's Garden shows the church across the valley, with Toompea and the city's spires behind it.
text.geographic_location: St Nicholas' Church stands in Tallinn's Old Town, in the Lower Town below the Toompea hill. The Kohtuotsa terrace is on the Upper Town side, looking down over it.
text.directions_text: Head for Tallinn Old Town and the Toompea hill. Kohtuotsa is on the Upper Town side, and the church lies to the south of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the spire and the roofs around it. Switch to the default lens (1x) if you want Toompea and more of the Old Town in the frame.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the spire on one of the vertical lines, with the roofs filling the lower part of the picture. Keep the phone level so the tower does not lean. For a different angle, try the view from the Danish King's Garden, across the valley.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the spire to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. If you zoom in, hold the phone with both hands against the railing or your body to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the terrace.

text.description:
St Mary's Cathedral, known in Estonian as Toomkirik, stands on Toompea hill in the medieval centre of Tallinn. It is the oldest church in Tallinn and in mainland Estonia, founded in the 13th century as a Catholic cathedral. It became Lutheran in 1561 and is now the seat of the Archbishop of Tallinn. The exterior dates from the 15th century, while the baroque spire on the western end was added in 1778-79. That mix of old stone and a later spire gives you a lot to look at.

It photographs best from the front. From the small open space in front of the building you get a straight-on view of the tower and white facade, with clean lines that suit a phone. The light is softest in the morning, and the space is quieter then, so you can frame the whole front without people crossing the shot. Keep the phone level, use the gridlines to keep the tower upright, and take a few frames at different distances. A step back usually gives the neatest composition.

If you want the Old Town rather than the cathedral, Kohtuotsa and the Bishop's Garden Viewing Platform are a short walk away. They make a good second stop, but the cathedral is barely in view from them.
text.geographic_location: On Toompea hill, in the medieval centre of Tallinn, on the street called Toom-Kooli. The cathedral is the oldest church in the area.
text.directions_text: Head for Toompea hill in Tallinn's Old Town; there is no station or tram stop at this spot, so make your way up to Toompea on foot from the Old Town. From there the cathedral is to the north, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Toom-Kooli (the frontage of the cathedral, the small open space in front of the building). A straight-on view of the cathedral's tower and white facade, best taken from the open space in front of the church. shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so the building does not lean. Keep the whole tower in the frame, with a little space above the spire. If you use the ultra-wide (0.5x), keep the phone level, because tilting it makes the building lean. For a different view, Kohtuotsa viewing platform gives a wide look over the Lower Town roofs, though the cathedral is not the subject there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white facade to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the walls keep their detail and are not washed out against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before about 9:00 in summer, when the square is quiet and the light comes from the east.

text.description: Tallinn's medieval city wall is one of the reasons the Old Town is a World Heritage Site, and much of it and many of its gates still stand today. The story starts in 1265, when Margaret Sambiria ordered the first wall, which was under 5 metres tall and about 1.5 metres thick at the base. It was strengthened and enlarged over the centuries, and in the fourteenth century townspeople were required to turn out for guard duty in their armour. For photographs, the best-known view is the row of red-roofed towers lined up along the wall. The small grassy park at the foot of the wall, Tornide väljak, gives a good ground-level angle on them, with greenery in the foreground to soften all that stone. Guides suggest late afternoon for the light. One guide also mentions an opening in the wall between Kooli and Laboratooriumi streets as the way to reach the aligned-towers view. If you want a different picture, Patkuli viewing platform shows a long stretch of intact wall with rooftops, St Olaf's spire and the harbour beyond. Müürivahe is a narrow lane where the tower facades rise straight above you. Take a few frames from the park first, then walk along the wall and try a tighter shot of one tower. Keep the phone level, as the towers look best when the vertical lines stay straight.
text.geographic_location: The wall runs around Tallinn's Old Town in the centre of the city, and the best-known row of towers is in the Old Town and Toompea area. The park at its foot, Tornide väljak, sits right beside the wall.

text.description: Alexander Nevsky Cathedral is the largest cupola church in Tallinn, and its five onion domes make it easy to spot on Toompea hill. It was built between 1894 and 1900, when Estonia was part of the Russian Empire, in the Russian Revival style, to a design by Mikhail Preobrazhensky. The base is Finnish granite and the domes carry gilded iron crosses. Inside there are eleven bells cast in Saint Petersburg, and the biggest weighs about 16 tons. The cathedral has a complicated place in Estonian history, and many Estonians have seen it as a symbol of Russian rule. It is also a working Orthodox church, so it is worth photographing with some respect. It photographs well because the shapes are so strong: the rounded domes, the pale decorated walls and the dark granite base give you clear layers even on a plain phone snap. Keep the whole building in view, then move in for a few detail shots of the domes and crosses. If people are coming and going, wait a moment for a clear gap rather than cropping them out later.
text.geographic_location: On Toompea hill in central Tallinn, in the upper part of the Old Town area, with the cathedral standing as the main landmark of the hill.
text.directions_text: Walk east from there and you will be facing the cathedral. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole cathedral. If the domes are cut off at the top of the frame, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the domes, crosses and decoration.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From here the whole building and its domes should be in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the vertical lines straight by holding the phone upright, not tilted back, so the walls do not lean. Place the cathedral on one side of the grid and leave a little sky above the highest dome. Then try a closer, zoomed shot of the five domes against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the pale walls and the sky keep their detail and the gilded crosses do not burn out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mid to late afternoon, when the sun is behind you and lights the side you are facing. Early morning also tends to be quieter.

text.access_note: The cathedral is an active place of worship, so expect to dress modestly inside; check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements.
